DOCUMENT:
Vendor Comparison: Standard Parcel Delivery Contract
Larkspur Home, Operations, June 2026

1. Purpose
Our contract with our current standard-delivery carrier ends on 30 September 2026. This paper compares three shortlisted carriers and recommends which should carry our standard (two-to-four-day) parcels from October.

2. Volumes and requirements
We dispatch an average of 42,000 standard parcels a month: about 70% weigh under 2 kg (cushions, textiles, small homeware) and 30% weigh 2 to 10 kg (lamps, mirrors, small furniture). Our requirements are on-time delivery of at least 95%, a damage rate below 0.5%, full tracking, and a returns service.

Damage and loss matter to us commercially. Each damaged or lost parcel costs us on average £48 in replacement stock, return shipping and customer service time, and damaged items are the most common cause of one-star reviews.

3. Trial
Between 1 April and 31 May 2026, each shortlisted carrier delivered a share of our orders, allocated at random by the warehouse management system, about 5,000 parcels per carrier. We measured on-time delivery against the promised date, damage reported by customers within 14 days, and lost parcels.

Table 1. Prices and trial performance
Carrier | Price, under 2 kg | Price, 2-10 kg | On-time delivery | Damage rate | Lost per 10,000 parcels
SwiftDrop | £3.10 | £4.60 | 96.2% | 0.4% | 3
ParcelLine | £2.85 | £4.95 | 93.1% | 0.9% | 8
Meridian | £3.30 | £4.40 | 97.5% | 0.3% | 2

On-time delivery was above 95% for all three carriers during the trial, and all three offer full tracking and a returns service.

4. Cost comparison
Applying our 70/30 weight mix, the average cost per parcel is £3.55 for SwiftDrop, £3.48 for ParcelLine and £3.63 for Meridian. On 42,000 parcels a month, the monthly cost would be £149,100 for SwiftDrop, £146,160 for ParcelLine and £152,460 for Meridian. ParcelLine is therefore the cheapest option, saving £2,940 a month against SwiftDrop and £6,300 a month against Meridian, or between about £35,000 and £76,000 a year.

5. Customer contact
"Where is my order?" contacts are our largest single category of customer service enquiry. During the trial, ParcelLine deliveries generated 6 such contacts per 1,000 parcels, compared with 11 for SwiftDrop and 10 for Meridian. ParcelLine's live-tracking app clearly reduces customer contacts, and at an average handling cost of £3.20 per contact this would save about £670 a month at our volumes. From 1 May, ParcelLine parcels also carried our new proactive delivery-day text message, which we were testing on one carrier before rolling it out.

6. Other considerations
All three carriers can collect from our warehouse daily at 6 pm. ParcelLine and SwiftDrop offer a 12-month contract; Meridian requires 24 months. SwiftDrop and Meridian have both handled our peak-season volumes for other retailers of similar size, while ParcelLine's references were mainly from fashion retailers with lighter parcels.

All three carriers integrate with our warehouse management system through standard interfaces, and none would require changes to our packing process or labelling. Each offers recipients a delivery-preference service to nominate a safe place or a neighbour, and each provides proof-of-delivery photographs, which our customer service team has found useful in resolving disputes.

7. Recommendation
ParcelLine offers the lowest delivery cost, met our service requirements in the trial and reduces customer contacts through its tracking app. We recommend awarding the standard parcel contract to ParcelLine for 12 months from 1 October 2026, saving up to £76,000 a year against the alternatives.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "On-time delivery was above 95% for all three carriers during the trial" -- Table 1 shows ParcelLine's on-time delivery was 93.1%, below the 95% requirement. The claim (and the recommendation that ParcelLine 'met our service requirements') misreads the table; ParcelLine's 0.9% damage rate also fails the stated 0.5% requirement.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "ParcelLine's live-tracking app clearly reduces customer contacts" -- The document states that from 1 May ParcelLine parcels alone also carried the new proactive delivery-day text message. That concurrent intervention confounds the comparison, so the lower contact rate cannot be attributed to ParcelLine's tracking app.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "ParcelLine is therefore the cheapest option, saving £2,940 a month against SwiftDrop" -- The cost comparison ignores the stated £48 cost of each damaged or lost parcel. ParcelLine's damage and loss rates (0.9% and 8 per 10,000) versus SwiftDrop's (0.4% and 3 per 10,000) imply about 231 extra problem parcels a month (about £11,100), far exceeding the £2,940 price saving; ParcelLine is likely the most expensive option overall.

REVIEW:
The price arithmetic is correct throughout. However, the recommendation contradicts the paper's own trial results. ParcelLine failed two of the four stated requirements, and once damage and loss costs are included, it becomes the most expensive option, not the cheapest. The customer-contact advantage is also confounded by a text-message test that ran only on ParcelLine parcels.

## Major issues

**1. ParcelLine missed the 95% on-time requirement.**
Table 1 shows ParcelLine at **93.1%**. Section 3's statement that "on-time delivery was above 95% for all three carriers" is incorrect, as is your description's "all three carriers cleared our 95% on-time threshold." Only SwiftDrop (96.2%) and Meridian (97.5%) met it. With about 5,000 parcels per carrier, a gap of roughly three points is very unlikely to be chance.

**2. ParcelLine also failed the damage requirement, by a wide margin.**
Section 2 requires a damage rate below 0.5%, and ParcelLine's was **0.9%**, nearly twice the limit and three times Meridian's. The paper never mentions this. It matters commercially: Section 2 says each damaged or lost parcel costs £48 and damage is the most common cause of one-star reviews.

**3. Including damage and loss reverses the cost ranking.**
Applying the paper's own £48 per damaged or lost parcel to 42,000 parcels a month:

| Carrier | Delivery cost | Damaged + lost parcels | Damage/loss cost | **Total per month** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SwiftDrop | £149,100 | 168 + 13 ≈ 181 | ≈ £8,670 | **≈ £157,770** |
| ParcelLine | £146,160 | 378 + 34 ≈ 412 | ≈ £19,760 | **≈ £165,920** |
| Meridian | £152,460 | 126 + 8 ≈ 134 | ≈ £6,450 | **≈ £158,910** |

On this basis ParcelLine costs about **£8,150 a month (≈ £98,000 a year) more than SwiftDrop**, and about £7,000 a month (≈ £84,000 a year) more than Meridian. Its £2,940–£6,300 price advantage is wiped out more than twice over by extra damage. This also leaves out the reputational cost of the additional one-star reviews.

**4. The drop in customer contacts can't be credited to ParcelLine's tracking app.**
Section 5 notes that from 1 May, ParcelLine parcels alone carried your new proactive delivery-day text message. That covers half the trial, so the lower rate of "where is my order?" contacts (6 per 1,000 against 10–11) could come from the text, the app or both. The text is being rolled out to all carriers anyway, so the benefit will probably apply whichever carrier you choose.

Even taking the paper's claimed saving of about £670 a month at face value, it's a small fraction of ParcelLine's extra damage costs. ParcelLine would still be about £7,500 a month more expensive than SwiftDrop. A fair comparison would use April data only, when no carrier had the text, or would test the text on all three.

## Smaller issues

- **Loss rates rest on very few parcels.** At about 5,000 parcels per carrier, 3, 8 and 2 per 10,000 correspond to roughly 1–2, 4 and 1 actual lost parcels. These figures shouldn't be given much weight on their own. The differences in damage and on-time rates are based on much larger counts and are more reliable.
- **Peak season risk.** The contract starts on 1 October, just before the Christmas peak. The trial ran in April and May, which are off-peak. ParcelLine's references are mainly from fashion retailers with lighter parcels. Your 30% share of lamps, mirrors and small furniture is exactly where the damage risk lies. SwiftDrop and Meridian have both handled similar peak volumes.
- **"Saving up to £76,000."** On delivery prices alone, the saving against SwiftDrop, the comparable 12-month option, is £35,000. The £76,000 figure is against Meridian, which has a 24-month term, so it isn't a like-for-like comparison. In any case, both figures disappear once damage is included.
- **The 12-month term isn't unique to ParcelLine.** SwiftDrop offers the same flexibility.

## What holds up

- The weighted prices: £3.55, £3.48 and £3.63 per parcel.
- Monthly costs of £149,100, £146,160 and £152,460, and the differences of £2,940 and £6,300 (£35,280 and £75,600 a year).
- The trial design, with random allocation by the warehouse system, is a strong basis for comparing on-time and damage performance. It just doesn't support the conclusion drawn from it.

## What the evidence actually supports

**SwiftDrop** looks like the strongest option:
- It meets all four requirements.
- It has the lowest total cost once damage and loss are included.
- It offers a 12-month term.
- It has experience at peak volumes.

**Meridian** has the best service figures and costs only about £1,100 a month more in total. It's a good alternative if you're willing to accept the 24-month term.

ParcelLine could only be reconsidered if it brought damage below 0.5% and on-time delivery above 95%, ideally backed by contractual penalties or liability for damage, and demonstrated that in a further trial.

## Suggested revisions

1. Correct the on-time statement and report ParcelLine's failure against the damage requirement.
2. Add a total-cost comparison that includes damage and loss at £48 per parcel.
3. Separate the effect of the text message from the carrier, or drop the claim about the app.
4. Reconsider the recommendation in light of these findings. On the current evidence it points to SwiftDrop.

In short, the trial was well designed, but its results argue against ParcelLine rather than for it. The carrier presented as cheapest and service-compliant failed two of the paper's own requirements and would cost roughly £100,000 a year more once damage is counted.
